title: Delivering Feedback to a Veteran Employee
script: Narrator: [measured] Giving critical feedback has never troubled me much when the recipient is new, but doing so with someone who trained me a decade ago is an entirely different matter.
Narrator: [reflective] Yusuf had been at the company for fifteen years, and his methods, while once cutting-edge, had quietly fallen behind the systems everyone else had since adopted.
Narrator: [honestly] I'd noticed it for months, but kept telling myself it wasn't my place to say anything, given how much I owed him professionally.
Narrator: [thoughtful] The problem was that his outdated approach had started slowing down two other teams, whose complaints were reaching me rather than him directly.
Narrator: [uneasy] I dreaded the conversation for a full week, rehearsing sentences in the shower that all sounded either condescending or unbearably vague.
Narrator: [determined] Eventually, I decided vagueness would be the greater disrespect, so I asked him to meet somewhere quiet, away from the rest of the floor.
Narrator: [explaining] I opened by acknowledging what he'd taught me, then explained specifically how his current process was creating bottlenecks for people downstream of his work.
Narrator: [nervous] For a moment he said nothing, and I genuinely thought I'd damaged something between us that wouldn't be repaired easily.
Narrator: [surprised] Instead, he exhaled and admitted he'd suspected as much, but had been too proud, or perhaps too tired, to ask anyone to walk him through the newer tools.
Narrator: [relieved] That admission changed the entire tone of the conversation, from correction into something closer to collaboration.
Narrator: [warmly] We spent the next hour mapping out which parts of his workflow could be updated without discarding the judgment his experience actually provided.
Narrator: [reflective] What struck me afterward was how much unnecessary suffering the delay had caused, both to him and to the teams quietly frustrated behind his back.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Respect, I've since decided, isn't protected by silence; if anything, silence eventually corrodes it, since problems left unspoken rarely resolve themselves.
Narrator: [peacefully] These days, whenever I catch myself avoiding a difficult conversation out of deference, I remind myself that Yusuf, given the choice, would rather have heard it sooner.

options: Yusuf had trained him a decade ago and had fifteen years at the company

quiz.explanation: The narrator explains Yusuf trained him a decade ago and had fifteen years at the company, making the feedback feel different.
